summary: Defines relationships for composing a complete path metric from metrics of its sub-paths, so end-to-end network performance can be estimated from measurements of the parts. This is called spatial composition in RFC 2330.

eli5.summary: If you know how long each leg of a trip takes, you can estimate the whole trip. This does the same for network delay and loss.

questions: what is spatial composition of metrics
how to compose packet loss from sub-paths
how to estimate end to end delay from sub-path measurements
subtitle: How to estimate a whole network path's delay, loss and delay variation from measurements of its parts.

tldr.problem: Often nobody can measure a complete source-to-destination path, for example because it crosses several independent domains with different policies, tools and timing.
tldr.mechanism: Each sub-path is measured separately, and defined functions combine the results: sum the mean delays, sum the minimum delays, combine loss probabilities, and combine delay variation distributions.
tldr.outcome: The result is an estimate of the complete-path metric, not a measurement. It is only as good as the stated assumptions, chiefly that sub-paths are sufficiently independent.

today: RFC 6049 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 6248. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Compose Metrics
sections.content:
The one-way delay and loss metrics from RFC 2679 and RFC 2680 assume you can measure directly between the source and the destination you care about. Sometimes that is not practical. The path may cross several independent domains that have conflicting policies, measurement tools and measurement timing.

This memo takes the other route, called spatial composition in RFC 2330. Each domain measures one sub-path in its own way, and the results are combined into an estimate for the complete path. The memo defines the deterministic functions that do the combining.

The RFC is candid that these relationships involve conjecture. For example, it does not expect delay singletons from each sub-path to sum to an accurate estimate of a singleton on the complete path, but other statistics based on a reasonable sample size may work in enough circumstances.
sections.eli5: You cannot always time a whole trip yourself, because it passes through lands run by different people. So each person times their own piece, and you add the pieces up.

sections.title: Scope, Application and Missing Data
sections.content:
The memo covers composed versions of the delay metric (RFC 2679), the loss metric (RFC 2680) and the delay variation metric (RFC 3393). The composition may use the same metric on every sub-path, several metrics per sub-path, or active and passive measurement techniques. Working backwards, to infer a missing sub-path from the complete path and the other sub-paths, is explicitly out of scope.

For each metric the memo states its applicable circumstances, as the composition framework in RFC 5835 requires. Questions include whether the same test packets must cross all sub-paths, whether measurement methods must match, whether the metric works across domains, and whether sub-path independence must be assumed.

If measurement cannot be started on a sub-path, the test result SHOULD be recorded as undefined. This differs from the case where packets were sent all interval and all were declared lost. If any sub-path result needed by a composed metric is undefined, the composed metric SHOULD also be recorded as undefined.
sections.eli5: If one friend forgets to time their piece of the trip, you do not guess. You write down 'unknown' for the whole trip. 'Unknown' is different from 'we sent letters and every single one got lost'.

sections.title: Common Parameters and Sources of Error
sections.content:
All the metrics use the Type-P naming convention from RFC 2330. Section 3 collects what they share: the source and destination addresses, the start and end of the test interval (T and Tf), a maximum waiting time Tmax that separates very late packets from lost ones, the number of packets sent M and received N, and the number of sub-paths S. A sample can be a Poisson stream or a Periodic stream, and both are RECOMMENDED.

The methodology SHOULD use similar packets sent and collected separately in each sub-path, and SHOULD have synchronized measurement intervals, though largely overlapping intervals MAY suffice. Assuming sub-path independence is REQUIRED.

The RFC lists where composition drifts from the ground truth:

  • Measurement packets may take a different route than packets on the complete path, for example because of Equal Cost Multi-Path or re-routing.
  • A sub-path may include extra elements, such as a dedicated link to a measurement system.
  • Sub-paths may not cover everything, such as an exchange point between two networks.
  • When no route exists, composition can still produce a finite estimate.

Encapsulation, encryption and fragmentation can also make complete-path packets behave differently from the sub-path test packets.
sections.eli5: Adding up the pieces only works if the pieces really cover the whole trip, and everyone takes the same road. If a friend took a shortcut or skipped a bridge, the total will be off.

sections.title: Composing Delay and Loss
sections.content:
Delay composition builds on a helper metric, Type-P-Finite-One-way-Delay, which is just the destination timestamp minus the source timestamp for packets that arrived. Counting only packets with finite delay avoids having to give lost packets an invented huge delay.

Two composed delay statistics follow. The composite mean is the sum of the mean finite delays of all S sub-paths. The composite minimum is the sum of the minimum delays of all S sub-paths. Both assume a large enough stream on each sub-path, sufficiently independent distributions and continuous delay distributions. The mean can mislead if a sub-path's distribution is multi-modal, and the minimum can come out too low for the current path if routing on a sub-path is unstable.

For loss, each sub-path yields an empirical probability of loss, Ep, the average of a per-packet loss indicator. The composition is CompEp = 1 - {(1 - Ep1) x (1 - Ep2) x ... x (1 - EpS)}. If any sub-path value is undefined for an interval, the composed value is undefined. The RFC warns that correlated causes break the assumption. A fire in a shared tunnel could hit several networks at once, and a fast-spreading worm can change loss in one network and so affect the next.
sections.eli5: For delay, add up each leg's time. For lost letters, work out the chance that a letter survives every leg, then flip it to get the chance it gets lost somewhere.

sections.title: Composing Delay Variation
sections.content:
The delay variation metric, Type-P-One-way-pdv-refmin, measures each packet's finite delay minus the minimum finite delay in the stream. That makes the distribution independent of the sending sequence. The RFC states it is equivalent to the IP Packet Delay Variation parameter in Y.1540. Defined statistics are the mean, variance, skewness and a quantile.

Because delay variation cannot simply be summed, two alternative ways to estimate a quantile of the complete path are given:

  • Approximate convolution: each sub-path's delay samples are summarized as a histogram with 1-ms bins, and the distribution of the sum of independent variables is computed from them.
  • Normal Power Approximation (NPA): the sub-path statistics are combined by the process in Y.1541, Clause 8 and Appendix X.

Both assume stationary, sufficiently independent sub-path distributions. If sub-path delay distributions are correlated, neither is a reliable estimator, and extreme outliers have increased error in practice. Very tight distributions, a few milliseconds wide, are not accurately represented by 1-ms bins, a size chosen on the view that errors of a few milliseconds are acceptable.
sections.eli5: You cannot just add up how bumpy each leg was. Instead you keep a tally of how often each leg was slow or fast, and combine the tallies to guess how bumpy the whole trip was.

sections.title: Security and IANA Registration
sections.content:
The measurement stream could be abused for denial-of-service attacks against the destination or intervening networks. The RFC advises bilateral or multilateral agreements among the networks about timing, size and frequency of samples. Active use generates its own packets, so it does not threaten user data. Passive measurement MUST restrict attention to the headers of interest and MUST protect any stored payloads; a hashing function is usually enough for payload comparison.

Someone who can recognize sample packets could treat them differently and distort the result, or inject extra packets that look like part of the sample. Packet interference checks such as a cryptographic hash may be used.

IANA registered the metrics in the IANA-IPPM-METRICS-REGISTRY-MIB, as identities 71 through 83 under ianaIppmMetrics.
sections.eli5: Someone could flood the road with test traffic, or give the test cars special treatment so the timing looks better than it is. So the networks agree on rules, and checks can spot cheating.

items.title: Mean delay
items.text: Sum of the sub-path mean finite delays.

items.title: Minimum delay
items.text: Sum of the sub-path minimum finite delays.

items.title: Packet loss
items.text: 1 minus the product of (1 - Ep) over all sub-paths.

items.title: Delay variation
items.text: Quantile from approximate convolution or the Normal Power Approximation.
